title: What Are REO Properties and How to Buy Them: A Complete Investor's Guide
excerpt: REO properties are bank-owned homes that failed to sell at foreclosure auction, and they can offer serious discounts for savvy investors. Learn exactly what REO properties are, how they work, and the step-by-step process to buy one successfully.

sections.content: If you've been hunting for discounted real estate deals, you've probably come across the term REO properties. They show up on bank websites, MLS listings, and investor forums constantly. But what exactly are they, and how do you actually buy one? REO stands for Real Estate Owned, which means the property is owned by a bank or lender after a failed foreclosure auction. For investors, REO properties can be one of the most reliable sources of below-market deals — if you know how to navigate the process. This guide breaks down everything you need to know. If you're also looking to expand your deal-finding strategy beyond REOs, check out our [complete guide to finding motivated sellers](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/finding-motivated-sellers) for a broader view of where the best opportunities are hiding.
What Are REO Properties?

An REO property is a home or building that a bank or mortgage lender has taken back after the borrower defaulted on their loan. Here's how it happens: A homeowner stops making payments, the lender files for foreclosure, and the property goes to a public auction. If no one bids high enough at the auction to cover the loan balance, the bank takes ownership of the property. At that point, it becomes "Real Estate Owned" — an asset sitting on the bank's books that they need to get rid of. Banks are not in the business of owning houses. They want to convert these properties back into cash as fast as possible, which is why REO deals often come with motivated sellers and real room to negotiate.
REO vs. Foreclosure: What's the Difference?

These two terms are often confused, but they refer to different stages of the same process. A foreclosure is the legal process where a lender tries to recover money on a defaulted loan. During this phase, the property may sell at a courthouse auction to the highest bidder. If it sells there, it's no longer a foreclosure — it belongs to whoever bought it. An REO property is what's left after that auction fails. The bank now owns it outright, with no mortgage attached. This is actually good news for buyers because REO properties come with a clear title, unlike some auction purchases that can carry liens or legal complications.
Why REO Properties Attract Investors

items: Discounted prices: Banks often price REOs below market value to move them quickly off their books
Clear title: Unlike tax lien or courthouse auction purchases, REO properties come with a clean title guarantee
No occupants: Most REO properties are vacant, which means no complicated eviction process
Negotiable terms: Banks may cover closing costs, accept lower offers, or negotiate repair credits
Volume opportunities: Large banks manage hundreds of REOs at once, giving experienced buyers repeat deal flow
Financing available: Unlike auction purchases that require cash on the spot, REO buyers can often use conventional financing

sections.content: "The best REO deals don't go to the fastest buyers — they go to the most prepared ones. Know your numbers, have your financing ready, and understand what the bank actually needs before you make an offer."
How to Find REO Properties

Finding REO properties takes a bit of legwork, but there are several reliable channels investors use every day. The most direct route is through bank and lender websites. Major institutions like Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and Fannie Mae (HomePath) list their REO inventory publicly. You can also find REOs on the MLS, where they're often listed by asset management companies hired by the bank. Sites like Hubzu, Auction.com, and RealtyTrac also aggregate REO listings. For government-backed loans, HUD.gov lists FHA-foreclosed properties that are sold through a sealed-bid process.

REO properties are technically on-market deals, but savvy investors combine REO hunting with off-market strategies to stay ahead of the competition. If you want to explore the full landscape, our guide on [how to find off-market real estate deals](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/off-market-real-estate-deals) covers complementary tactics like driving for dollars, probate leads, and direct mail. Speaking of driving for dollars — if you spot a vacant, neglected property while scouting a neighborhood, it could be a pre-foreclosure heading toward REO status soon. Our [driving for dollars guide](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/driving-for-dollars-guide) walks you through exactly how to turn those sightings into deals.

Pro Tip: Set up free alerts on Fannie Mae's HomePath website and your local MLS for new REO listings in your target zip codes. Properties priced at the steepest discounts often go under contract within the first 48-72 hours, so speed matters.
How to Buy an REO Property: Step by Step
Step 1: Get Pre-Approved or Proof of Funds Ready

Before you make a single offer, have your financing locked in. Banks will not take your offer seriously without a pre-approval letter from a lender or a proof of funds letter if you're paying cash. REO asset managers review dozens of offers at once — an incomplete offer gets thrown out immediately. If you're planning to use a hard money loan, have that commitment letter ready as well.
Step 2: Run Your Numbers Before You Fall in Love with a Deal

This is where most new investors get hurt. REO properties are often sold as-is, meaning the bank won't make repairs or give you credits for problems discovered after closing. You need to estimate repair costs accurately and know your maximum allowable offer before you bid. A good rule of thumb for wholesalers and flippers is the 70% rule: don't pay more than 70% of the after-repair value (ARV) minus repair costs. For example, if a property's ARV is $250,000 and needs $40,000 in repairs, your max offer would be $135,000. Use the free [Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to run these numbers quickly and make sure every deal pencils out before you commit.
Step 3: Submit Your Offer Through the Right Channels

REO offers are almost always submitted through a licensed real estate agent who has access to the asset management portal or MLS listing. You'll fill out the bank's standard purchase contract (not a typical state contract in many cases) and submit it with your pre-approval or proof of funds. Include a reasonable earnest money deposit — typically 1-2% of the purchase price — to show you're serious. Banks generally respond within 3-5 business days, sometimes longer for larger portfolios.
Step 4: Complete Your Due Diligence Fast

Once you're under contract, move quickly. Most REO contracts give you a short inspection window — often 10 days or less. Hire a licensed home inspector and walk the property yourself. Check the roof, foundation, HVAC, plumbing, and electrical. Look for signs of water damage, mold, or structural issues. Remember: the bank will not negotiate much after this point, so if the inspection reveals major surprises that blow up your numbers, you may need to walk away and protect your earnest money.
Step 5: Close and Take Ownership

REO closings follow a standard process, but they move on the bank's timeline. Don't expect a quick 2-week close — 30 to 45 days is more realistic, and some institutional sellers take longer. Once you close, the property is yours free and clear with a clean title. From there, you execute your exit strategy: flip it, rent it, or wholesale it to another investor.
Combining REO Deals with Other Lead Sources

The sharpest investors don't rely on just one source of deals. REOs are excellent, but competition can be fierce in hot markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx), and [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az). To build a more consistent pipeline, pair REO hunting with other lead-generation strategies. Properties with code violations, for example, are often owned by distressed landlords or absentee owners who may be heading toward foreclosure. Our guide on [finding sellers from code violation lists](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/code-violation-property-list) shows you exactly how to pull these lists from your city and use them to get ahead of the REO process entirely. Similarly, if you locate a promising REO property but need to reach a related party — an heir, an executor, or a previous owner — [skip tracing](https://aiwholesail.com/blog/skip-tracing-real-estate-guide) gives you the tools to track down contact information quickly.

If your long-term goal is building wealth without being hands-on, REO properties can also be a gateway into buy-and-hold investing. A discounted REO in a strong rental market can produce solid cash flow for years. Our guide on [passive real estate investing](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/passive-real-estate-investing) covers how to build that kind of portfolio systematically.
Common Mistakes to Avoid with REO Properties

items: Skipping the inspection: Never skip a professional inspection just because the deal looks good on paper
Underestimating repair costs: Banks sell as-is, and deferred maintenance is often worse than it looks at first glance
Submitting low-ball offers without justification: Banks use automated valuation tools — an offer that's too far below list price will be ignored without a written repair estimate to back it up
Ignoring the bank's addenda: Bank contracts often override standard state contracts with terms that heavily favor the seller — read every page
Assuming REO always means deep discount: In competitive markets, REO pricing can be close to retail once you factor in competition and bidding wars
